title: Monty Hall problem
lede: The Monty Hall problem is a probability puzzle about a game show: you pick one of three doors, the host opens another to show a goat, and you may switch. If the host always knowingly reveals a goat, switching wins the car two times in three.

sections.heading: The puzzle
sections.body:
The puzzle is named after Monty Hall, the original host of the American game show [[Let's Make a Deal]] [1]. The statistician Steve Selvin first posed it in a letter to *The American Statistician* in 1975 [2]. It became famous in 1990, when a reader's version ran in [[Marilyn vos Savant]]'s "Ask Marilyn" column in *Parade* magazine [3]. The rules:

1. There are three closed doors. One hides a car, two hide goats.
2. You pick a door, but it stays closed.
3. The host, who knows where the car is, opens one of the other two doors and shows a goat.
4. He offers you the last closed door instead of yours.

Should you switch? Most people say it makes no difference. It does.

sections.heading: Why switching wins
sections.body:
Under the standard rules, switching wins the car with probability 2/3 and staying wins with probability 1/3 [1]. The short reason: when you first pick, there is a 2/3 chance the car is behind one of the two doors you did not choose [2]. The host then opens the one of those two that has a goat, so all of that 2/3 ends up on the door he leaves closed.

Say you pick door 1. There are only three places the car can be, each equally likely [3]:

| Car is behind | Host opens | Staying gets | Switching gets |
|---|---|---|---|
| Door 1 | door 2 or 3 | car | goat |
| Door 2 | door 3 | goat | car |
| Door 3 | door 2 | goat | car |

Switching wins in two of the three rows. Put another way, switching loses only when your first guess was right, and your first guess is right one time in three.

Vos Savant made the same point with more doors: "Suppose there are a million doors, and you pick door #1" [4]. The host, who knows where the prize is, opens every other door except one. Nobody thinks their first blind pick is the one that survived. Try it below with up to 100 doors.

sections.heading: What the host knows
sections.body:
The 2/3 answer is not a fact about doors. It is a fact about the host's rule, and the numbers depend on how the host and the player choose their doors [1]. The *Parade* version did not actually say that the host always opens a door, always offers a switch, or never reveals the car [2]. That gap is where much of the argument about the puzzle lives.

Change one thing: the host does not know where the car is and opens one of the other two doors at random. This variant is called "Monty Fall" or "Ignorant Monty", and when the door he opens happens to show a goat, switching wins only half the time [3].

Count it out. In a third of games your first pick is the car. In the other two thirds, a blind host opens the car half the time, which ruins a third of all games. What remains is one third where staying wins and one third where switching wins: a tie.

The two hosts can show you the same goat behind the same door. The difference is that the knowing host was never going to show you the car, so his choice carries information about the door he skipped. The random host's choice carries none. The simulation below runs 10,000 games under each rule.

sections.heading: The 1990 column and the letters
sections.body:
Vos Savant has written "Ask Marilyn" for *Parade* since 1986, and the column is what made the puzzle widely known [1]. She answered that the contestant should switch. By her estimate the magazine then received 10,000 letters, close to 1,000 of them signed by people with PhDs, most saying her answer was wrong [2]. *Parade* ran four columns on the problem in all [3].

The skeptics included [[Paul Erdős]], one of the most prolific mathematicians of the twentieth century, who stayed unconvinced until he saw a computer simulation produce her result [4]. The same test is the cover of this page: play enough games and the tally settles near 2/3 for switching.

sections.heading: Why it fools people
sections.body:
The common answer is that two closed doors must mean a 50% chance each [1]. That would be right if you were choosing between the two remaining doors at random, with no history. But switching is a different act: it uses what the host's choice told you, and a blind choice does not [2].

The puzzle has a reputation for beating experts. The cognitive psychologist Massimo Piattelli-Palmarini wrote that "no other statistical puzzle comes so close to fooling all the people all the time" [3]. Pigeons do better: in experiments, pigeons that play the game repeatedly quickly learn to always switch, while humans do not [4].

sections.heading: The same reasoning elsewhere
sections.body:
The trap, treating a piece of evidence as if it arrived at random when it did not, is older than the game show.

- **[[Bertrand's box paradox]]** (Joseph Bertrand, 1889) [1]. Three boxes hold two gold coins, two silver coins, and one of each. You draw a gold coin from a random box. The chance the other coin in that box is gold is 2/3, not 1/2.
- **[[Three Prisoners problem]]**. Published by Martin Gardner in 1959, it is the Monty Hall problem with the car and goats replaced by a pardon and executions [2].
- **[[Bayes' theorem]]**. The formal solution multiplies the prior odds on each door by how likely the host was to open the door he did if the car were there [3]. A knowing host who could not open door 2 and chose door 3 gives door 2 twice the odds of your door. A random host gives no such tilt.

Bridge players meet the same idea as the [[Principle of restricted choice]], another application of this kind of Bayesian updating [4]. Underneath all of them is [[Conditional probability]]: what you should believe depends on how the evidence was produced, not only on what it shows.
